news.title: Vibe genes? Natural(ish) language comes to protein, genome design software
news.summary: Protein design tools may be getting increasingly sophisticated, but you still need a sophisticated understanding of protein structure for them to work. This can include knowing enzyme mechanisms down to the positions of specific amino acids, as well as the water molecules that also occupy the area where catalysis takes place. Once you specify these, the tools can build the rest of a protein around this target. A large collaboration of researchers based in China, however, decided to bring protein design to the masses, making a tool that can take natural language prompts and use them to produce proteins with the function you specify. If your measure for success is a working protein, then the success rate may not be great. But they still manage to get the job done.

news.title: How AI Is Changing the Pace of Discovery for Millions Living With Dementia
news.summary: There are 57 million people worldwide living with dementia today. For the researchers working to help them, the obstacle isn’t a lack of effort — it’s too much data, too few experts to synthesize it and a pace of discovery that can’t keep up with the disease. The Consortium for Biomedical Research and AI in Neurodegeneration (C-BRAIN), working with NVIDIA, is using AI to change that. Alzheimer’s disease is one of today’s leading global health challenges, with over 10 million new dementia cases diagnosed each year. Despite a 7x increase in National Institutes of Health funding in the last 15 years — reaching $3.9 billion annually — no treatment has been found to stop, prevent or reverse the disease yet. The bottlenecks are not enough high impact scientific findings, too much data living in institutional silos and too slow a pace of synthesis to keep up with the research that is published.

news.title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
news.summary: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it. That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management, scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability. For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it.

news.title: Inside cohere model vault building verifiable confidential ai inference
news.summary: In Cohere's product launch, Cohere introduced Confidential Computing on Cohere Model Vault, now in public beta with NVIDIA GPUs on Microsoft Azure. This article goes deeper into how the system works. The goal is not simply to encrypt inference. It is to reduce the infrastructure that customers must trust with plaintext data and give them cryptographic evidence they can verify before sensitive information is released. That requires more than a confidential virtual machine. A confidential inference system has to protect the computation itself, the path that carries sensitive requests to it, and the mechanism customers use to decide whether the destination can be trusted.

news.title: Introducing confidential computing on cohere model vault
news.summary: Today, Cohere is announcing the public beta of Confidential Computing on Cohere Model Vault, bringing hardware-backed protection and independently verifiable security to managed enterprise AI. Model Vault gives enterprises dedicated, fully managed model inference. With Confidential Computing, Cohere is extending that experience to some of an organization's most sensitive workloads and data, including financial information, clinical records, privileged documents, proprietary source code, and intellectual property. The goal is simple: enterprises should be able to use the capabilities and operational simplicity of managed AI without giving the infrastructure that operates it access to their sensitive plaintext data. Encryption traditionally protects data in two places: while it is stored and while it travels across a network. Confidential Computing on Model Vault is designed to protect the third state: data in use.
